How to roll this system out to a team: who hears what, in what order, and what the first quarter looks like. The story itself, the questions people ask and how growth feels are in [02 Why digital services](/system/why-digital-services). This document is the sequence.

## When

- **Start eight to ten weeks before the first quarter.** Leaders first, then partners, then the team, then each practice right before it is first used.
- **The first quarter is a rehearsal.** Plan it, run it, and expect it to be messy.
- **Review the system itself at the end of every quarter,** at the quarter review and the retro that follows.

## Who

- **Sponsor** (a member of the executive steering group): opens the leadership session, names the steering group, and backs the cut-off line when it bites.
- **Change lead** (usually the product manager, or whoever is installing the system): owns this plan, runs the leadership, partner and kickoff sessions, and collects what breaks.
- **Scrum master**: runs the practice trainings for planning and sprints, and the team's retros.
- **Product owner**: runs the triage training and the first triage reviews.
- **Functional managers**: hear the model before their staff do, so one-on-ones reinforce it instead of contradicting it.
- **Process improvement owner**: keeps the system documents current. Changes from a quarter's retro go to them.

## How it works

### 1. Go in order: leaders, partners, team, practice

| Step | Audience | Deck | What it should leave behind |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Leadership session | Executive steering group, functional managers | From Request Fulfillers to Outcome Owners | Agreement on the why. A named steering group and advisory group. A date for the first direction review. |
| 2. Partner introduction | Advisory group, partner managers, frequent requesters | A New Way of Working | Partners know how to work with the team: how requests get an answer, when planning happens, what they will hear and when. |
| 3. Team kickoff | The whole team | Team Kickoff: A Vision for Our Future | The vision, the roles, what starts now, and the red flags written down. |
| 4. Working agreement | The whole team | None: a working session | A first team agreement, written as situations in time order, updated whenever someone hits a confusion point. |
| 5. Practice trainings | The people who run each practice | One deck per practice, below | Each practice taught right before its first use. |

Don't skip step 1 to get to the team faster. A team that hears the model before its managers and steering group have agreed to it will be told two different things in the same week.

### 2. Teach each practice right before the team first uses it

| Practice | Deck | Run it |
|---|---|---|
| Request triage | How Requests Are Reviewed | The week before the first weekly triage. It can start before the first quarter, and it is the fastest visible win. |
| Mapping and slicing | How We Map and Slice the Work | Before the planning week, so candidate Solutions arrive in pieces small enough to size. |
| Quarterly planning | How We Plan the Quarter | Day 1 of the planning week, before the first session. |
| Sprints and the sprint report | How We Run a Sprint | The week before Sprint 1 planning. |
| Discovery | How We Learn Before We Build | When the first Initiative goes active and discovery starts on it. |

Training weeks ahead of first use is wasted: people forget it before they need it. "This is a lot" is the honest close for every one of these sessions.

### 3. Treat the first quarter as a rehearsal

- **Commit anyway.** Teams new to planning don't know how to commit yet, and the first quarter can miss. Committing is how the team learns to.
- **Say what isn't ready.** Some prep that normally happens before planning won't be done the first time. Say so at the start of the planning week.

### 4. Know what "working" looks like by when

| By | What should be true |
|---|---|
| The kickoff | Steering and advisory groups named. Every request channel points to one intake form. |
| The first quarter starts | Triage has run at least twice and every requester heard back. Quarterly commitments are written and each person committed out loud. |
| Sprint 1 review | The first sprint report row exists, with a sprint goal and a yes or no. |
| The first month | The first steering and advisory meetings have happened and changed something you can point to. |
| The end of the quarter | The quarter review has marked each commitment Done or rolled forward. The team has held a retro on the system itself. |

If one of these is missing, that is where to spend the next two weeks, not on the next practice.

### 5. Watch where people are

Check the growth zones in [02](/system/why-digital-services) at retros and one-on-ones. Most of the team in comfort means nothing is changing. Several people in distress means the rollout is moving faster than they can absorb: slow down and drop a practice for a quarter rather than push.

### 6. Change the system on purpose

At the end of each quarter, the team holds one retro on the system itself: what to keep, what to change, what to drop. The change lead takes the changes to the process improvement owner, who updates the documents and says what changed. A team that adapts the system without writing it down ends up with a different system in every room.

## Template

**Rollout plan**

| Field | What goes here |
|---|---|
| Team | Who is adopting the system, and the service they run |
| Sponsor and change lead | Names and roles |
| Leadership session | Date, attendees, and the decisions it must produce |
| Partner introduction | Date and who is invited |
| Team kickoff | Date |
| Working agreement | Date, and where the agreement lives |
| Practice trainings | One line per practice: date, who runs it, and the first use it prepares for |
| First quarter | Planning week, quarter dates, first triage, Sprint 1 start |
| Checkpoints | The "working" checks above, with dates |
| System retro | Date, and who updates the documents afterward |

## DMV example

**Rollout plan: DMV digital service team**

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Team | The DMV digital service team: product manager, product owner, scrum master, UX designer and researcher, content strategist, technical architect, development team |
| Sponsor and change lead | Deputy director (sponsor). Product manager (change lead) |
| Leadership session | Oct 22. Steering group named that day; advisory group invited by Oct 31; direction review set for November |
| Partner introduction | Nov 5, with field office managers, the call center lead and the records unit |
| Team kickoff | Nov 13 |
| Working agreement | Nov 20, kept on the team's wiki and updated at each retro |
| Practice trainings | Triage: Nov 26, product owner, before the first triage on Tuesday Dec 3. Mapping and slicing: Dec 4, product owner, before planning week. Quarterly planning: Dec 9, scrum master, morning of day 1. Sprints: Jan 3, scrum master, before Sprint 1. Discovery: early April, product manager, when Single-trip new driver licenses goes active |
| First quarter | Planning week Dec 9-12. Quarter Jan 6 to Mar 31. Sprint 1 starts Jan 6 |
| Checkpoints | Two triage reviews before Jan 6. First sprint report row on Jan 17. First advisory and steering meetings Jan 21 and Jan 28. Quarter review Mar 31 |
| System retro | Mar 31, after the quarter review. The product manager takes the changes to the process improvement owner |

What the first system retro changed: the team agreed to bring the latest sprint report to the monthly steering meeting rather than send it separately, and to write the reason on any small request marked urgent after two jumped the line without one.

## Rules of thumb

- Leaders first. A team should never hear the model before its managers have agreed to it.
- Teach just in time. A practice taught weeks before its first use is forgotten by then.
- Start with triage. Every requester getting an answer is the first change people outside the team will notice.
- The first quarter is a rehearsal. A plan and a habit beat a perfect plan.
- One change at a time is still a lot. Remember 10% and repeat.
- Change the system on purpose, and write the change down.
